transcript.heading: News Report One (American Male)
paras: A new community event called "Repair Café" is gaining popularity in cities across Canada, where volunteers help people fix broken household items for free instead of throwing them away. At these monthly events, held in community centers and libraries, people can bring everything from broken toasters and blenders to torn clothing, bicycles, and small furniture. Skilled volunteers - including electricians, tailors, carpenters, and bicycle mechanics - donate their time to make repairs and teach owners how to fix items themselves. Since the first Repair Café opened in Toronto three years ago, the movement has spread to twenty cities across the country, repairing over twelve thousand items and keeping an estimated twenty-five tons of waste out of landfills. Organizers say the events also build community connections, bringing together neighbors who might not otherwise meet and passing along practical skills that are becoming less common in today's throwaway culture.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Female)
paras: A new smartphone application launched in the United Kingdom is helping households reduce food waste by connecting neighbors who have surplus food with people who can use it. The app, called "FoodShare," allows users to list extra food they have - whether it's groceries they won't use before expiration, leftover prepared meals, or produce from home gardens - and other users in the same neighborhood can request it for free. Since its launch six months ago, over eighty thousand people have signed up, and users have shared over one hundred thousand meals' worth of food that would otherwise have been thrown away. The app also includes tips for food storage, recipe suggestions for using leftovers, and information about local food banks. Experts estimate that the average UK household wastes around six hundred pounds worth of food annually, so apps like this could make a significant difference in reducing food waste while also helping people save money and build community connections.
Questions 3 and 4 are based on the news report you have just heard.
3. How many people have signed up for the app since launch?
4. How much food does the average UK household waste annually?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (British Male)
paras: A children's hospital in London has introduced a therapy dog program to help young patients feel more comfortable and less anxious during their hospital stays. The program uses five specially trained golden retrievers and their handlers who visit the hospital wards several times a week, allowing children to pet, play with, and read to the dogs. Medical staff report that children who interact with the therapy dogs show lower heart rates and blood pressure, require less pain medication, and are more cooperative during medical procedures. Parents also say the dogs help children feel less scared and lonely in the hospital environment. The program has been so successful that the hospital plans to expand it by adding three more dogs and extending visits to the emergency department and outpatient clinics. Other hospitals across the UK are now looking to introduce similar programs after seeing the positive results in London.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Female + British Male)
paras: Woman (Megan): Hey Ben, did you hear about the university's public speaking competition next month?
Man (Ben): Hi Megan, I saw the posters but I didn't read the details. What's it about?

Woman: It's open to all undergraduate students. You have to give a five-minute speech on a topic related to sustainability and the environment. The first prize is five hundred pounds and your speech gets published in the university magazine.
Man: That sounds interesting, but I get really nervous speaking in front of people. I could never do that.
Woman: That's exactly why I'm thinking about doing it - I want to overcome my fear of public speaking. I'm terrible at it right now - my voice shakes and I forget what I'm going to say.
Man: But what if you freeze up on stage? That would be so embarrassing.

Woman: Sure, it might be. But I figure the only way to get better is to practice. The competition is also offering free workshops for participants to help you prepare and improve your speaking skills.
Man: Free workshops? That's actually really helpful. What would you talk about?

Woman: I'm thinking about the Repair Café movement - we had one in my hometown, and it's such a simple idea but it really reduces waste and builds community. I think it's a good example of a small, practical solution that could be scaled up.
Man: That's a great topic! But five minutes isn't very long - you'd have to be really focused.
Woman: I know, I'd have to practice a lot to keep it concise. Are you sure you don't want to do it too? You could talk about something related to your environmental science major.
Man: I don't know... I do have strong opinions about reducing plastic waste - that's a topic I could speak passionately about. But I don't know if I could get up on stage.
Woman: Think about it this way - even if you don't win, just participating would help you become more confident. And we could practice together!
Man: Hmm, you make a good point. When is the deadline to sign up?
Woman: Next Friday. Let's both register - if we're both terrible, at least we'll be terrible together.
Man: Okay, fine. Let's do it. But you owe me a coffee if I freeze up on stage.
Woman: Deal!
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.
8. What is the topic of the speeches in the competition?
9. What topic is the man considering for his speech?
10. Why does the woman hesitate to participate?
11. When is the registration deadline?

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (American Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Ethan): Zoe, I need your advice. I'm having problems with my roommate and I don't know what to do.
Woman (Zoe): Oh no, Ethan. What's going on? I thought you and Lily got along well.

Man: We do, mostly. The problem is that she never cleans up after herself in the kitchen. She leaves dirty dishes in the sink for days, spills things on the counter and doesn't wipe them up, and she always leaves her food in the fridge until it goes moldy.
Woman: That sounds really frustrating. Have you talked to her about it?

Man: I've mentioned it a few times, but she just apologizes and cleans up for a day or two, then goes right back to her old habits. I don't want to be mean or make living together awkward, but I'm tired of cleaning up her messes.
Woman: I understand. It's hard to live with someone who has different standards of cleanliness. Have you tried making a cleaning schedule?
Man: I suggested that at the beginning of the semester, but she said she's too busy with classes and her part-time job to stick to a schedule.
Woman: What about setting up some kind of chore chart where you split up tasks? Or maybe having a weekly cleaning session together?

Man: I don't know... she might think that's too strict. The thing is, I'm not the neatest person in the world either, but basic cleanliness is important to me, especially in the kitchen where we prepare food.

Woman: Maybe you could frame it differently - not that she's messy, but that you feel stressed when the apartment is dirty, and you'd really appreciate it if you could both make an effort. Sometimes people respond better when you talk about your feelings rather than criticizing their behavior.
Man: That's a good idea. I've just been saying "you need to clean up" which sounds accusatory. I should try using "I" statements instead.
Woman: Exactly. Like "I feel uncomfortable when there are dirty dishes in the sink for days" instead of "you never clean your dishes." People get defensive when they feel attacked.
Man: You're right. What if that doesn't work?

Woman: If she still doesn't change, you might have a more serious conversation about whether you're compatible as roommates. But hopefully it doesn't come to that. Most people are willing to compromise if you approach them nicely.
Man: Thanks, Zoe. That's really helpful advice. I'll talk to her tonight after class, when we're both relaxed.
Woman: Good luck! I hope it goes well. Let me know how it turns out.
Man: I will. Fingers crossed!
Questions 12 to 15 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

13. Why did the roommate reject the cleaning schedule idea?
14. What communication approach does the man recommend?

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Female)
paras: When people think of bees, they often think only of honey and painful stings, but these small insects play an absolutely critical role in global food production and ecosystem health. Bees are the world's most important pollinators, responsible for pollinating approximately one-third of all food crops that humans eat, including fruits, vegetables, nuts, and many oilseed crops. Without bees, foods like apples, almonds, blueberries, strawberries, tomatoes, and chocolate would become extremely rare and expensive, significantly impacting global nutrition and food security.

Unfortunately, bee populations around the world have been declining at an alarming rate over the past two decades. Beekeepers in Europe and North America typically report losing thirty to forty percent of their honeybee colonies each winter, compared to historical rates of around ten to fifteen percent. Wild bee species are also in decline, with some species facing extinction. Scientists attribute this decline to a combination of factors: habitat loss as wild areas are converted to farmland or development, widespread use of certain pesticides that are toxic to bees, diseases and parasites carried by mites, and climate change, which disrupts the timing of when flowers bloom and when bees emerge from hibernation.

The good news is that there are simple things everyone can do to help bees. Planting a variety of native flowers that bloom throughout the growing season provides bees with the nectar and pollen they need to survive. Avoiding pesticides in home gardens, leaving patches of bare ground for ground-nesting bees, and even putting up bee hotels for solitary bees can make a difference. Supporting organic farming practices and buying local honey from beekeepers who use sustainable methods also helps protect bee populations. Protecting bees isn't just about saving an insect - it's about protecting our food supply and the health of ecosystems that support all life, including humans.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Male)
paras: Libraries have existed for thousands of years, from ancient clay tablet collections in Mesopotamia to the great Library of Alexandria, but their role in society has changed dramatically over time, and they continue to evolve today. Traditionally, libraries were primarily repositories of books and knowledge - places to store written materials and make them available to scholars. For centuries, libraries were among the few places where ordinary people could access books, which were rare and expensive before the invention of the printing press.

The modern public library movement of the 19th century made free library access available to all people, regardless of class or income, recognizing that access to knowledge is essential for an educated, democratic society. Libraries added fiction reading rooms, children's sections, and reference services staffed by librarians who could help patrons find information. The 20th century brought new formats - record collections, films, audiobooks on cassette, and eventually CDs and DVDs - as libraries expanded beyond just printed books.

Today's libraries are transforming more rapidly than ever in response to digital technology. While books remain central, modern libraries offer computers and internet access for people who don't have it at home, digital media lending, 3D printers, maker spaces, job search assistance, English language classes, tax preparation help, and community meeting rooms. Many libraries now lend tools, musical instruments, toys, kitchen equipment, seeds for gardening, and even Wi-Fi hotspots - things completely unrelated to traditional library materials. Far from becoming obsolete in the digital age, libraries are becoming more important community hubs, adapting to meet the changing needs of their communities while remaining true to their core mission: providing free, equal access to information, resources, and opportunity for everyone.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (British Female)
paras: If you're looking for a simple, free way to improve your physical health, boost your creativity, and improve your mood, you might not need to join a gym or start an expensive new hobby. The solution could be as simple as going for a walk. Walking is one of the most accessible forms of exercise, requiring no special equipment or training, and research increasingly shows it offers remarkable benefits for both body and mind.

Physically, regular walking strengthens the heart, improves circulation, lowers blood pressure, and helps maintain healthy bones and muscles. Just thirty minutes of brisk walking most days of the week reduces the risk of heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, and certain types of cancer. Unlike high-impact exercises like running, walking is gentle on the joints, making it suitable for people of all ages and fitness levels. Walking also helps with weight management and improves sleep quality.

The mental and creative benefits of walking are equally impressive. Numerous studies have found that walking - especially walking outdoors in natural settings - reduces stress, anxiety, and symptoms of depression by lowering stress hormone levels and releasing endorphins, the brain's natural mood boosters. Research from Stanford University has shown that walking increases creative thinking by up to sixty percent compared to sitting, because walking increases blood flow to the brain and allows the mind to wander freely, making new connections between ideas. Many famous writers, artists, and thinkers - from Charles Darwin to Steve Jobs - used long walks to help them think and generate new ideas.

You don't need to walk for hours or go long distances to get benefits. Short ten-minute walks throughout the day add up, and even a brief walk around the block can help clear your mind and improve your focus when you're feeling stuck on a problem. Walking with a friend adds social connection, another important factor for health and wellbeing. In a world that increasingly encourages sitting - at desks, in cars, in front of screens - making time for walking is a simple but powerful investment in your overall health.
